name: Microsoft Translator
oneLine: Microsoft's free app for iPhone and Android that translates speech, text and photos; its store listings say multi-device conversations have been retired.

platforms.detail: The App Store lists it for iPhone and iPad, and Google Play has the Android app. Microsoft says its Windows desktop app is retired.

deviceRequirements.text: iOS 17 or later; Android not stated
deviceRequirements.detail: The US App Store listing needs iOS 17.0 or later (iPadOS 17.0 on iPad). The Google Play listing doesn't show a minimum Android version.

roomCaptions.detail: The microphone translates what is said between two chosen languages, hands-free when both support auto-detect. In auto mode each speaker can talk for up to 20 seconds (Android FAQ), and Microsoft doesn't describe captions in the same language.

groupConversations.detail: Both store listings say the multi-device conversation feature has been retired (App Store version 26.7.1, June 30, 2026). Some Microsoft pages still describe joining a conversation from several phones with a code; a split-screen mode puts two people on one phone.

languages.detail: Microsoft's languages page marks 48 languages for speech (Levantine Arabic on Android only) and 135 for text; the store listings say over 100. Its Android FAQ still says 11 speech languages.

offline.detail: Microsoft says speech translation works only while online. With downloaded language packs, text and photos translate without internet.

speakerLabels.detail: Microsoft's current pages don't describe showing who is talking. Split-screen mode gives two people one phone, one language each.

translation.detail: Speech is translated between two chosen languages, and the app detects which one is spoken when both support it. A split-screen mode lets two people share one phone.

saveTranscripts.detail: Recent translations stay in the app's history and can be pinned or saved as favourites. Transcripts were part of the conversation feature (2023 blog); the store listings now say the multi-device conversation feature has been retired.

export.detail: Translations can be copied, sent as a text message, or shared by email or social apps. No transcript file export is described.

fileUpload.detail: Microsoft says the app doesn't translate media or files such as movies or video clips. You can upload photos to translate the text in them.

summaries.detail: No AI summaries are described for the app. Microsoft's 2023 blog mentioned meeting topics in the conversation feature's transcripts.

customWords.detail: No option to add your own words or names is described.

display.detail: Microsoft's app pages don't describe text size or colour options.

videoCalls.detail: Captioning Zoom, Teams or Meet calls isn't described for the app.

mediaOnDevice.detail: Microsoft says the app doesn't translate media or files such as movies or video clips.

humanCaptioners.detail: No human captioning option is described.

signLanguage.detail: No sign language feature is described.

privacy.detail: Speech works only online, so it goes to Microsoft's service. The iOS FAQ says speech isn't collected unless you agree to share voice clips; Microsoft's privacy statement says sampled audio is de-identified before it's used to improve the service.

account.detail: Microsoft says the app doesn't need you to sign in.

availability.detail: Microsoft's pages don't list country limits; which features work depends on the language.

freePlan.detail: Microsoft says the app is free of charge, and the App Store lists it as Free.

price.detail: No paid plan or in-app purchases are listed on the US App Store (October 2026), and Microsoft's FAQ says the app is free.

accessibilityFunding.detail: No funding programme is needed: the app costs nothing.

strengths.text: Free, with no account or sign-in needed.
Speech translation in 48 languages and text translation in 135, by Microsoft's language list.
Detects which of two languages is spoken, so two people can talk without tapping the microphone each time.
Downloaded language packs translate text and photos without internet.

limits.text: Both store listings say the multi-device conversation feature, which Microsoft promoted for deaf and hard of hearing students, has been retired (June 2026).
Speech translation works only while online.
It doesn't translate media or files such as movies or video clips.
In auto mode each speaker can talk for at most 20 seconds (Android FAQ).

sources.title: Translator for iOS FAQs
quotes: No, the Microsoft Translator app doesn’t require you to be authenticated (e.g., with a user ID and password).
By default, the speech translation data is not collected. Data is collected only if you consent to contribute voice clips.
Voice clips of 20 seconds are collected by the Microsoft’s Speech service
If you see a microphone with stars, it means you can speak in any of the 2 languages selected, and the app will auto-detect your spoken language and translate it to the other language.
Speech translation feature works only while online.
The Microsoft Translator app does not support translation of external media sources or files, such as movies or video clips.
The Microsoft Translator App is free of charge.
All your favorite translations are saved in “Favorite” section.

sources.title: Translator for Android FAQs

Speech conversations using the live conversation feature, and short-form translations using the single microphone and split-screen microphone feature are currently not available while offline.
For in-person conversations with another person, you can use the Microsoft Translator split-screen feature to translate your conversation using a single device.
Currently Microsoft Translator supports 11 speech languages.
To view all of your saved translations, tap the clock icon on the Home screen.
How to send a translation as a text message

quotes: Turn on the Presenter mode toggle in the multi-device conversation feature Settings pane while giving a presentation.

sources.title: Transitioning the Microsoft Translator web app to a simplified experience (August 3, 2022)
quotes: This means that the ability to start and host a conversation from the web app will be removed and the preset conversation feature will be retired.
The session join process will remain the same wherein participants simply need to input the five-character code, visit the host’s URL, or scan the host’s QR code to join the session.

sources.title: Introducing the redesigned Microsoft Translator app for iOS (February 28, 2023)
quotes: We have incorporated a new AI technology in Cognitive Services, continuous Language Identification (LID), into speech translation where two people can have natural and continuous conversations without the interruption of selecting source/target audio languages or tapping the microphone each time someone speaks.

Use the conversation feature by tapping on the icon located on top-right corner of the app to transcribe a single person’s speech or translate multiple users within a group. Stay on top of conversations by accessing the transcripts and using meeting topics to navigate within a transcript.
View your translation history on the same page as you continue translating new phrases.

sources.title: Microsoft Translator for Education
quotes: Teachers manage many types of learners, including students who are deaf or hard of hearing (DHH) who require assistive technology
The Translator app's conversation feature helps teachers better communicate with students in class or for one-on-one conversations.

sources.title: Live conversations - Education - Microsoft Translator
quotes: The Translator multi-device conversation feature helps English language learners, deaf, or hard-of-hearing students or parents communicate with one another in class or for one-on-one chats.
* The Microsoft Translator app for Windows desktop is retired and is no longer available for download from the Microsoft Store.

sources.title: Microsoft Privacy Statement (Last Updated: September 2026), section Microsoft Translator
quotes: Microsoft Translator processes the text, image, and voice data you submit, as well as device and usage data, to provide translations, personalize your experiences, and improve our products and services.

Microsoft uses business and technical measures designed to help de‑identify submitted data — such as deleting identifiers and certain text like email addresses and some number sequences that could contain personal data — when randomly sampling text and audio for product improvement.
Microsoft Privacy, Microsoft Corporation, One Microsoft Way, Redmond, Washington 98052, USA.

notes: Status of the conversation feature: both store listings (App Store version 26.7.1, June 30, 2026; Google Play updated June 29, 2026) say 'The multi-device conversation feature has been retired.' Microsoft's own web pages have not caught up: the app features page, the Education pages and the multi-device conversation help page (all opened 2026-10-28) still describe hosting or joining conversations. I found no Microsoft blog post or support article announcing the retirement (the Translator blog's newest post is from December 2023); only the store release notes. A press piece (WhistleOut) gave June 30, 2026 as the date; not used as a source. translator.microsoft.com (the old web join site) now returns 301 to microsoft.com/translator, so there is no web join page. microsoft.com/en-us/translator/live.aspx returned 403. Language counts: 48 speech / 135 text are my count of the Yes marks in the table on microsoft.com/translator/languages (136 rows; one row, Arabic (Levantine), is speech-only and Android-only). The page has no stated total. The Android FAQ's '11 speech languages' conflicts with it and looks out of date; the stores say 'over 100 languages' (text). Whether the single-phone split-screen and auto-detect conversation still exist after the June 2026 update is from the FAQ pages, not re-verified in the app. Privacy wording differs: the iOS FAQ says speech data is not collected by default, while the privacy statement says Microsoft randomly samples de-identified text and audio for product improvement; both reported. The privacy statement still lists a Windows app, which Microsoft retired. Speaker names, display options and Android minimum version were not stated on any page I opened. Cleaned 2026-10-28: store listings re-opened that day; App Store version history shows 26.7.1 (Jun 30) with the retirement note, Google Play 'Updated on Jun 29, 2026'. Microsoft's app features page still lists the multi-device conversation feature ('Translate and caption live conversations'). Speech/text counts recounted from the languages table: 48 and 135. Neither store shows in-app purchases.
